content_html:
Removing smoke odor requires identifying what burned and which surfaces absorbed residue. Ventilation helps with stale air, but cooking smoke, fireplace smoke, or a minor fire can remain in textiles, walls, filters, and settled dust, so cleanup needs to move from source to surfaces.

Remove the source and ventilate when outdoor air is suitable

Remove burned material or ash once it is cold and safe, and create cross-ventilation when outdoor air is clean. Do not use fans to spread smoke while an active fire or electrical hazard exists.

Clean textiles and surfaces according to material

Curtains, covers, bedding, and carpet retain odor; follow care labels and vacuum loose residue before wet cleaning where appropriate. On walls and furniture, test compatible cleaners and work from top to bottom.

Replace filters that captured smoke

heating and cooling system and air-purifier filters can collect smoke particles and later contribute odor or restrict airflow. Replace or clean them according to the manufacturer and do not use a filter more restrictive than the system supports.

Significant fire smoke needs deeper assessment

Visible soot across many surfaces, odor that persists after cleaning, or heavily contaminated porous materials may need professional restoration. A fire can also damage wiring, insulation, or finishes even when odor is the most noticeable symptom.
